title: Design a Todo List
statement:
Design a class `TodoList` that keeps to-do tasks for many users.

- `TodoList()` starts with no tasks.
- `addTask(userId, taskDescription, dueDate, tags)` gives user `userId` a new, unfinished task with that description, due date and list of tags, and returns the task's id. Ids are shared by all users and count up from `1`: the first task ever added gets id 1, the second gets 2, and so on.
- `getAllTasks(userId)` returns the descriptions of all of that user's unfinished tasks, sorted by due date from earliest to latest. It returns an empty list when there are none.
- `getTasksForTag(userId, tag)` returns the same kind of list, but only for the user's unfinished tasks whose tags include `tag` (exact, case-sensitive match).
- `completeTask(userId, taskId)` marks task `taskId` as finished, provided a task with that id exists, belongs to `userId` and is still unfinished. In every other case it changes nothing.

No two tasks share a due date, so every list has exactly one correct order.
constraints: Every string contains only English letters (either case) and digits
At most 100 calls are made to each method

signature.name: TodoList
methods: int addTask(int userId, String taskDescription, int dueDate, List<String> tags)

notes:
## Intuition

Each method needs a different view of the same tasks. Completing a task arrives with just an id, so a map from id to task makes that a single lookup, and storing the owner on the task lets us refuse a completion by the wrong user. The two list queries ask for one user's tasks in due-date order, so a second map from user to that user's tasks, kept sorted by due date, turns each query into one filtered pass. A simpler version keeps one flat list of everything and sorts the matching rows on every query; that is the brute force.

## Approach

1. Keep `nextId` (starting at 1), `taskById` (id → task) and `tasksByUser` (user → that user's tasks).
2. `addTask`: build a task object with its id, owner, description, due date, a `Set` of tags and `done = false`. Bump `nextId`, file the task in both maps, re-sort the user's list by `dueDate` and return the id.
3. `getAllTasks`: take the user's sorted list (or an empty one), drop finished tasks and return the descriptions.
4. `getTasksForTag`: the same, also requiring `task.tags.has(tag)`.
5. `completeTask`: look the id up in `taskById`; only if it exists and its `userId` matches, set `done = true` (setting it again is harmless).

## Example 1, step by step

Task 1 (`Task1`, due 50) and task 2 (`Task2`, due 100, tag `P1`) go to user 1, so `getAllTasks(1)` gives `["Task1", "Task2"]` and user 5 has `[]`. Task 3 (`Task3`, due 30, tag `P1`) is sorted to the front, so the `P1` query gives `["Task3", "Task2"]`. `completeTask(5, 1)` is ignored because task 1 belongs to user 1; `completeTask(1, 2)` finishes `Task2`. Now the `P1` query gives `["Task3"]` and `getAllTasks(1)` gives `["Task3", "Task1"]`.

## Complexity

- Time: `addTask` is O(k log k) for a user with k tasks (the sort), the two queries are O(k), and `completeTask` is O(1).
- Space: O(total tasks + total tags).

## Pitfalls

- Ids are global, not per user: a second user's first task can have id 2.
- `completeTask` must check the owner; a matching id alone is not enough.
- Finished tasks stay stored but must be left out of both queries.
- Tags compare exactly: `P1` and `p1` are different tags.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `nextId` | id the next added task will get |
| `taskById` | map from task id to its task object |
| `tasksByUser` | map from user id to that user's tasks, sorted by due date |
| `task` | one task: `id`, `userId`, `taskDescription`, `dueDate`, `tags` (a Set) and `done` |
| `tasks` | the list of the user being handled |
